paragraphs: Maximum cardinality bipartite matching pairs members of two sets while making as many pairs as possible, without reusing a member. This paper studies a geometric version: points in two planar sets may be paired only when their distance is within a chosen threshold. Such matching problems support calculations of bottleneck matchings and several distances between probability distributions.

The authors simplify a recent matching algorithm and show how to exploit this geometric setting. For moderately dense point sets, their method computes a maximum matching asymptotically faster than the n-to-the-three-halves running time discussed for the classical Hopcroft–Karp approach. The density qualification matters: the stated improvement is tied to that class of inputs.

For points drawn uniformly at random from a unit square, the paper gives an exact bottleneck matching algorithm taking roughly n-to-the-four-thirds time, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Experiments suggest that Hopcroft–Karp takes roughly n-to-the-three-halves time in this setting. The resulting execution-time improvements become substantial for larger inputs, connecting the theoretical speedup to a practical computational benefit.
neurips-2021-a-faster-maximum-cardinalit.tldr: A simplified geometric matching algorithm improves running time for moderately dense planar point sets and accelerates exact bottleneck matching on uniformly random inputs.

paragraphs: Bandit multiple testing combines two decisions: which possibilities to investigate next, and which ones have enough evidence to count as discoveries. Each arm represents a hypothesis. The statistical challenge is to find many genuine discoveries while controlling the false discovery rate, which concerns the proportion of reported discoveries that are mistaken.

The paper separates exploration from evidence assessment in a modular framework. Its central tool is an e-process, a martingale-based way of accumulating statistical evidence. This construction supports false discovery rate control across arbitrary composite null hypotheses, exploration strategies, and stopping times. It also accommodates dependent rewards, simultaneous queries to several arms, and multiple agents collecting observations.

In the previously studied setting of independent, sub-Gaussian rewards with one arm queried at a time, the framework matches existing sample complexity guarantees and performs comparably or better empirically. Its broader result concerns validity, not a universal sampling budget. Outside that special setting, the number of observations needed depends on the hypotheses, exploration strategy, dependence, and stopping rule; the paper does not analyze those sample complexities.
neurips-2021-a-unified-framework-for-ban.tldr: A modular framework separates adaptive exploration from evidence assessment to control false discoveries across a broad range of bandit testing settings.

paragraphs: A backdoored neural network can behave normally on ordinary inputs yet deliberately misclassify inputs containing a hidden trigger. This creates a risk when training is outsourced: a returned model may appear useful while carrying malicious behavior. Repair is especially difficult when the defender does not know what the trigger looks like.

The paper identifies a sensitivity that helps expose this behavior. When neurons are adversarially perturbed, backdoored networks are more prone to collapse and predict the attacker’s target label even on clean inputs. The authors use this observation to develop Adversarial Neuron Pruning, or ANP. The method removes some sensitive neurons to eliminate the injected backdoor.

Experiments show effective backdoor removal with very little clean data, including a reported example of only 1%, without obvious performance degradation. The finding suggests that sensitivity inside the model can provide a useful repair signal when the trigger is unknown. The reported outcome is empirical: ANP’s value is demonstrated through successful repairs while retaining ordinary predictive performance in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-adversarial-neuron-pruning-.tldr: Adversarial Neuron Pruning uses backdoored networks’ sensitivity to neuron perturbations to remove backdoors with very little clean data.

paragraphs: Weighted regression adjusts how strongly training examples influence a prediction model. Its performance can deteriorate when few examples are available or when input variables are perturbed. Reweighting the observations offers a way to address these problems, but it also raises a design question: how should the allowed changes in weights be organized?

This paper proposes a kernel-reweighted regression scheme that represents sample weights through a doubly non-negative matrix. It then confines that matrix to an uncertainty set defined using either log-determinant divergence or Bures–Wasserstein distance. These choices make the range of admissible reweightings an explicit part of the regression problem, rather than leaving sample importance fixed.

For these uncertainty sets, the authors show that the adversarially reweighted estimate can be computed efficiently using first-order optimization methods. This computational result matters because a robustness formulation must also be tractable to use. Numerical experiments across numerous datasets produce promising results, supporting the proposed weighting strategy without establishing that it improves every regression problem or every kind of input perturbation.
neurips-2021-adversarial-regression-with.tldr: A matrix-based formulation makes adversarial sample reweighting for kernel regression efficiently solvable under two specified uncertainty measures.

paragraphs: Agents learning together may improve more quickly by reusing one another’s policies, but useful transfer requires deciding whose behavior to borrow and when to stop borrowing it. The Multiagent Policy Transfer Framework, or MAPTF, treats these decisions as an option learning problem. A transferred policy becomes a behavior that an agent can select and later terminate.

Partial observability complicates this process because the option module must learn from agents’ local experiences. Those experiences may disagree, making estimates of a transferred policy’s value inaccurate or unstable. The authors address this with successor representation option learning, which separates environmental dynamics from rewards and evaluates options according to each agent’s preferences.

The framework can be combined with existing deep reinforcement learning and multiagent reinforcement learning methods. Experiments show significant performance improvements for existing methods in both discrete and continuous state spaces. The contribution is therefore more than sharing policies: it supplies a learned selection and termination mechanism, together with a way to evaluate transferred behavior when agents experience the environment differently.
neurips-2021-an-efficient-transfer-learn.tldr: MAPTF learns which agent’s policy to reuse and when to stop, while accounting for differences in agents’ experiences and preferences.

paragraphs: An image counterfactual explains a classifier by changing an input so that the predicted class changes in a desired way. To be useful, the change should be visible and interpretable while the resulting image remains realistic. This paper considers the setting where the trained classifier is available but its original training data are not.

The authors build on deep model inversion, which synthesizes images using information contained in a trained model. They show that existing inversion methods, despite their usefulness for conditional image synthesis, are insufficient for meaningful counterfactual explanations. Their method, DISC, adds stronger image priors, an objective promoting consistency with the data manifold, and a progressive optimization strategy.

Together, these components aim to produce an explanation tied to a particular query image, with realistic changes that affect the prediction. The reported counterfactuals are visually meaningful, effective for learning classifier decision boundaries, and robust to unknown corruptions at test time. These findings give the generated images a role both in explaining individual predictions and in understanding the classifier’s broader decision behavior.
neurips-2021-designing-counterfactual-ge.tldr: DISC generates meaningful image counterfactuals from a trained classifier without its training data by improving deep model inversion.

paragraphs: Soft articulated bodies combine deformation with coordinated motion, making their physical behavior important for both simulation and control. This paper develops a differentiable simulator for such systems. Differentiability allows simulated dynamics to participate in gradient-based optimization, so a learning or estimation procedure can use how outcomes change when its inputs or parameters change.

The method introduces a top-down matrix assembly algorithm within Projective Dynamics. It also develops a generalized dry-friction model for soft continua using a new matrix splitting strategy. These simulation components support a differentiable control framework for bodies actuated through muscles, joint torques, or pneumatic tubes, covering several ways to drive a soft articulated system.

Experiments report more stable and realistic soft-body simulation than other frameworks. The method also accelerates system identification, the estimation of system properties, by more than an order of magnitude. It enables efficient gradient-based learning of soft-robot motion control. The results connect improvements in physical simulation to faster estimation and usable control learning within the same differentiable framework.
neurips-2021-differentiable-simulation-o.tldr: A differentiable soft-body simulator improves physical simulation and supports faster system identification and gradient-based motion control.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent needs other signals to decide what to explore. Curiosity and transition-count approaches can help, but they may also respond to information unrelated to environmental dynamics, such as white noise. That sensitivity can make irrelevant variation appear worth investigating.

The paper proposes a Dynamic Bottleneck model that uses the information-bottleneck principle to obtain a representation relevant to dynamics. On top of this representation, DB-bonus rewards exploration of state-action pairs with high information gain. The design links the exploration incentive to information about the system’s behavior, addressing the distraction caused by dynamics-irrelevant observations.

The authors establish theoretical connections between DB-bonus and upper confidence bounds in the linear case, and between DB-bonus and visiting counts in the tabular case. These connections relate the new bonus to established exploration ideas under specific settings. Experiments on Atari environments with dynamics-irrelevant noise show that DB-bonus outperforms several leading exploration methods. The stated empirical benefit concerns robustness of exploration in those noisy environments.
neurips-2021-dynamic-bottleneck-for-robu.tldr: Dynamic Bottleneck learns dynamics-relevant representations and uses information gain to improve exploration in environments containing irrelevant noise.

paragraphs: Agents that communicate successfully with familiar partners may struggle with unfamiliar agents or people. Training a population of interacting agents can encourage more broadly usable communication, but the paper argues that earlier population methods achieved unfamiliar-partner coordination mainly with simple languages. Their ability to adapt to human partners using natural language remained a problem.

The authors attribute this difficulty to static populations and propose a dynamic population-based meta-learning approach. The population is built iteratively as part of training. This makes the construction of the partner population part of the learning method, with the goal of preparing agents for communication across familiar, unfamiliar, and human partners.

Evaluation on two referential games shows that the agents outperform prior work in communication with seen partners and humans. Separate analysis finds stronger natural-language generation than strong baselines. The study also tests communication with agents outside the population and examines individual components through ablations. The stated superiority for seen partners and humans should be distinguished from these additional robustness investigations, for which the abstract gives no equally broad ranking claim.
neurips-2021-dynamic-population-based-me.tldr: Iteratively building an agent population through meta-learning improves natural-language coordination with familiar partners and humans in two referential games.

paragraphs: Classification results can be summarized by accuracy, F-measure, and many other scores. Choosing among them raises a deeper question than which number looks best: what behavior should an evaluation measure have? This paper approaches that question by formally specifying desirable properties and examining which existing measures satisfy them.

The analysis establishes an impossibility result: some of the desired properties cannot hold simultaneously. Within this framework, selecting a measure therefore requires accepting a tradeoff. The theorem gives a precise reason why searching for a score with every listed virtue cannot succeed, rather than treating disagreements between measures as merely a matter of taste.

The authors then propose a family of measures satisfying every desired property except one. It contains the Matthews Correlation Coefficient and Symmetric Balanced Accuracy, which they identify as previously unused in classification literature. The practical contribution is a systematic basis for choosing evaluation measures. Users can relate a score’s mathematical behavior to their evaluation needs, while recognizing the unavoidable compromise established by the analysis.
neurips-2021-good-classification-measure.tldr: A formal analysis reveals unavoidable tradeoffs among classification metrics and proposes a family satisfying all but one of the specified desirable properties.

paragraphs: Automatically choosing a graph neural network architecture can reduce the effort of designing one for each task. This paper investigates how gradient-based architecture search makes those choices. Its measurement study finds that search tends to favor architectures according to how useful different types of information are for the target task.

The same investigation finds that noise in the graph can distort this process and lead to suboptimal architectures. The proposed method, GASSO, therefore combines differentiable architecture search with graph structure learning. It uses gradient descent to search the architecture while adapting the graph structure through a denoising process, jointly optimizing both parts.

This coupling matters because the graph supplying evidence to the search is itself subject to improvement. Architecture selection can therefore proceed alongside efforts to remove misleading structure, rather than depending on the original graph throughout. Experiments on real-world graph datasets report state-of-the-art performance against the evaluated baselines. Those results support the value of jointly searching the model and refining its graph input.
neurips-2021-graph-differentiable-archit.tldr: GASSO jointly searches graph neural network architectures and denoises graph structure to reduce the influence of graph noise on architecture selection.

paragraphs: Some learning tasks optimize a network’s input, such as finding a latent code that produces a target image or an input perturbation that worsens classification. Ordinarily, each optimization step requires a full forward and backward computation. Deep equilibrium models introduce a related expense: their output is obtained by solving for a fixed point of a nonlinear layer.

The paper combines these two computations by observing that gradient-based input optimization can itself be expressed as a fixed-point iteration. An augmented equilibrium model encodes both the original network and the optimization process. It solves for the network state and improves the input together, avoiding the naive arrangement of repeatedly solving a separate equilibrium problem for each input update.

The resulting speed improvement is sufficient to make training practical for tasks with an inner optimization loop. Demonstrations include generative modeling with optimized latent codes, denoising and inpainting, adversarial training, and gradient-based meta-learning. The contribution is a shared computational formulation: inference and input optimization become one coupled equilibrium problem, enabling more efficient use of equilibrium networks across these tasks.
neurips-2021-joint-inference-and-input-o.tldr: An augmented equilibrium network jointly solves inference and input optimization, substantially speeding tasks that otherwise require repeated inner optimization.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis reconstructs low-rank matrix structure while detecting outliers. The paper targets high-dimensional versions of this problem, where an approach needs both effective recovery and scalable computation. It introduces Learned Robust PCA, or LRPCA, as an efficient, learnable non-convex method.

LRPCA uses deep unfolding to learn free parameters of its optimization procedure. This connects an iterative algorithm with a neural network whose parameters can be trained to improve optimization. The authors also introduce a mixed feedforward and recurrent architecture, extending unfolding beyond a fixed finite sequence of iterations to an infinite-iteration formulation. This broadens how the learned iterative process can be represented.

The paper establishes a recovery guarantee under assumptions described as mild for robust PCA. That guarantee gives conditional theoretical support alongside the learned design. Numerical experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art methods, including ScaledGD and AltProj, on synthetic data and real-world applications. Together, these results support LRPCA as a scalable approach that combines trainable optimization parameters with a formal recovery analysis.
neurips-2021-learned-robust-pca-a-scalab.tldr: LRPCA combines learnable non-convex optimization with an extended deep-unfolding architecture for scalable robust matrix recovery and outlier detection.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through spikes, while their desired outputs are often ordinary labels or images. Training commonly bridges this mismatch by prescribing target spike patterns. That choice also implicitly fixes how spikes will be decoded, potentially restricting the network’s ability to use information carried by the timing of spikes.

The paper replaces a handcrafted decoding rule with a learned decoder. Its hybrid variational autoencoder combines a spiking neural network encoder with an artificial neural network decoder. The decoder learns to translate the encoder’s spike output into the target natural signal, making that translation part of the training problem.

The authors introduce an end-to-end learning rule that optimizes a directed information bottleneck objective through surrogate gradients. This provides a way to train the two components together while addressing the information represented by the spike sequence. Experiments across several tasks, including real-life datasets, demonstrate applicability. The stated result is evidence that learned decoding can support this hybrid architecture, rather than a claim of universal superiority across spiking-network tasks.
neurips-2021-learning-to-time-decode-in-.tldr: A hybrid autoencoder learns to decode spike timing into ordinary outputs instead of fixing the decoding rule through handcrafted target spikes.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether knowledge already embedded in large language models can help train a symbolic reasoning engine. Its central idea is that language captures some structure of the world, giving the learner a useful starting bias. That bias may help it learn reasoning behavior quickly and extend that behavior to related situations.

The authors study abstract reasoning expressed through text, including object manipulation and navigation. They demonstrate several forms of generalization to new scenarios and the symbols used within them. The motivating example is learning about stacking blocks and extending that understanding to other objects: linguistic knowledge can provide relationships that make such transfer natural.

The study also examines compositional learning, in which training on relevant simpler tasks helps a learner master a complicated task. The reported advantage shows that the choice of training tasks can complement the language model’s existing knowledge. Together, the findings support using pretrained language knowledge as an inductive bias for the examined reasoning problems, with generalization demonstrated through new textual situations and symbols.
neurips-2021-leveraging-the-inductive-bi.tldr: Knowledge in large language models helps symbolic reasoning engines learn and generalize, while relevant simpler tasks can improve learning of complex tasks.

paragraphs: Sampling from a complicated probability distribution and estimating its normalizing constant can both be difficult. NEO introduces importance-sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods built around an invertible transformation. Starting from proposal samples, the methods combine weighted points obtained by applying that transformation forward and backward.

The transformation does not preserve the target distribution, which motivates the name Non-Equilibrium Orbits. NEO-IS produces unbiased estimates of the normalizing constant and self-normalized importance-sampling estimates of expectations. NEO-MCMC combines multiple normalizing-constant estimates with an iterative sampling-and-resampling mechanism to sample from the target. The unbiasedness claim applies specifically to the normalizing-constant estimates.

When the transformation is a discrete-time integrator of a conformal Hamiltonian system, the authors report state-of-the-art importance-sampling performance on difficult benchmarks and successful exploration of highly multimodal targets with NEO-MCMC. The paper also provides theoretical results for both methods. Under mild conditions, it establishes uniform geometric ergodicity and explicit mixing-time estimates for NEO-MCMC, giving conditional guarantees about convergence as well as empirical evidence.
neurips-2021-neo-non-equilibrium-samplin.tldr: NEO uses weighted forward and backward trajectories of an invertible transformation to estimate normalizing constants and sample complex distributions.

paragraphs: Strong text generators do not automatically provide a convenient way to enforce explicit rules during generation. A task may require particular source words to appear, or may impose other constraints and prior knowledge. Earlier approaches often handle a particular rule through a specially designed model component or a specialized decoding procedure.

The paper proposes the Neural Rule-Execution Tracking Machine, or NRETM, as a module that can be added to different transformer-based generators. It uses multiple rules simultaneously to guide generation within a unified framework. This addresses the difficulty of building separate mechanisms case by case and then making several of them work together.

Experiments on several benchmarks support the module’s effectiveness in both controllable generation and general text generation. The reported benefit therefore extends beyond the narrow setting of producing text under explicit constraints. The contribution is a reusable way to incorporate rule execution into transformer generation, with empirical improvements across the examined tasks. The abstract presents this as effective guidance rather than a formal guarantee that every generated output satisfies every possible rule.
neurips-2021-neural-rule-execution-track.tldr: NRETM adds a reusable module to transformer generators so multiple rules can guide text generation together.

paragraphs: Programs communicate both what operations mean and how those operations are organized. This paper formulates program-guided tasks, in which a model learns to execute a supplied program on an observed task specification. The broader aim is a general program executor that brings perception, reasoning, and decision making into a shared framework.

The proposed Program-Guided Transformer, or ProTo, incorporates both semantic and structural guidance. Cross-attention and masked self-attention pass information between the task specification and routines in the program. Execution occurs in a learned latent space, giving the model a representation-based way to carry out the program. The authors describe this as offering stronger representation ability than earlier neural-symbolic approaches.

Experiments report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods on GQA visual reasoning and 2D Minecraft policy learning. ProTo also shows better generalization to unseen, complex, and human-written programs. These findings support the usefulness of treating program meaning and organization as complementary guidance, across both a visual reasoning task and a task requiring learned behavior.
neurips-2021-proto-program-guided-transf.tldr: ProTo uses program semantics and structure to guide transformer-based execution, improving visual reasoning, policy learning, and generalization to new programs.

paragraphs: Normalization methods that avoid dependence on a batch can perform worse than batch normalization. This paper investigates why, focusing on layer normalization and instance normalization. It identifies distinct failure modes in pre-activations, the values entering activation functions, connecting normalization choices to changes in what a network can express.

The authors find that layer normalization encourages collapse toward functions that are constant within channels. Instance normalization instead reduces variability in instance statistics, a symptom of altered expressivity. These observations motivate Proxy Normalization, which normalizes post-activation values using a proxy distribution. Its aim is to alleviate the first failure mode without worsening the second.

Combined with layer normalization or group normalization, Proxy Normalization remains independent of the batch while emulating batch normalization’s behavior. The authors report that these combinations consistently match or exceed batch normalization’s performance. The result connects a diagnosis of representational problems to a targeted normalization change: adjusting post-activations can help retain useful behavior without requiring normalization to depend on other examples in a batch.
neurips-2021-proxy-normalizing-activatio.tldr: Proxy Normalization uses a proxy distribution to normalize post-activations, helping batch-independent methods match or exceed batch normalization’s reported performance.

paragraphs: A predictor can fail in a new domain when it relies on correlations that change between training and deployment. This paper seeks a latent causal factor that supports prediction across such shifts. Its Latent Causal Invariance Models, or LaCIM, explicitly describe a causal structure and a source of variation between domains.

LaCIM introduces two correlated hidden factors: a causal factor and other information. A domain variable controls the extent of their correlation. Within this model, the authors prove that the distribution of observed variables conditional on the latent factors stays invariant across shifts. They then use this invariance to establish recovery of the causal factor without mixing in the other information, yielding the underlying prediction mechanism.

The authors develop a variational Bayesian method to learn the invariance for prediction. Experiments on several real-world datasets show improved generalization under distributional shifts. The theoretical recovery result is grounded in the proposed causal model, while the experiments provide evidence of practical usefulness. Together, they link an explicit explanation of domain changes to a method for learning more transferable predictive information.
neurips-2021-recovering-latent-causal-fa.tldr: LaCIM models domain-dependent correlations between hidden factors to recover causal predictive information and improve generalization under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Standard certifiable local robustness rules out adversarial changes within a small input neighborhood. The paper argues that strict separation between every pair of labels can be unnecessary for some tasks. If an image contains subjects from two classes, for example, either class might be an acceptable label, making a rigid boundary between them an awkward objective.

The authors introduce two alternatives. Relaxed top-k robustness provides a robustness counterpart to top-k accuracy. Affinity robustness specifies which label sets require a separating robustness margin and which may occur close together in input space. These properties let the safety requirement reflect acceptable relationships among labels while retaining a formal certification objective.

The paper shows how to construct models that can be efficiently certified for these relaxed properties and trained with little overhead beyond standard gradient descent. Experiments on several classification problems report lower rejection rates and higher certified accuracies than standard local robustness certification. These gains concern the newly defined safety properties: relaxing unnecessary label separation changes what is certified, allowing certification to better fit the task.
neurips-2021-relaxing-local-robustness-0.tldr: Two relaxed robustness properties allow task-appropriate relationships among labels while supporting efficient certification and improved reported certified accuracy.

paragraphs: Lookahead search improves decisions by considering what could happen next. Many successful game-playing systems use tabular search, but explicitly handling a large search space becomes difficult as that space grows. Randomness and partial observability make this scaling problem worse, motivating a different way to perform planning during decision making.

The paper replaces tabular search with online, model-based reinforcement learning that fine-tunes a policy neural network. Planning thus updates the network used to choose actions, using a model as part of the online learning process. The key change is the computational form of search: policy improvement through neural-network training takes the role previously served by tabular search.

In benchmark settings, the approach outperforms state-of-the-art search algorithms. The authors report a new state-of-the-art result in self-play Hanabi and an improvement over tabular search in Ms. Pacman. Results in these two games support the method’s applicability beyond a single benchmark. They demonstrate that online policy fine-tuning can serve as an effective planning mechanism in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-scalable-online-planning-vi.tldr: Online model-based reinforcement learning fine-tunes a policy network for planning, outperforming tabular search in Hanabi and Ms. Pacman benchmarks.

paragraphs: Wasserstein autoencoders compress data into a latent representation and use that representation to regenerate data. This paper studies the statistical basis of that process. It addresses a gap between the empirical success of autoencoders and the comparatively limited theoretical analysis of their ability to recover an input distribution after compression.

The first part establishes statistical guarantees that a Wasserstein autoencoder reaches its target distribution in latent space. The analysis uses Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory. This focuses on distributional consistency of the compressed representation, providing a formal foundation for reasoning about what happens when the model maps data into its latent space.

The main result then uses optimal transport under the Wasserstein metric to ensure regeneration of the input distribution. The argument connects consistency in latent space with distributional recovery after decoding. The study also offers indications about which classes of distributions can be reconstructed after compression into a latent law. Its contribution is a statistical account of distribution regeneration, rather than a new empirical comparison of generated samples.
neurips-2021-statistical-regeneration-gu.tldr: The paper provides statistical guarantees linking Wasserstein autoencoders’ latent distribution consistency to regeneration of the input distribution.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse tells someone what changes could lead to a favorable prediction, such as approval of a loan application. Such advice is often computed as though the predictive model will remain fixed. In practice, models are updated, and a change that would satisfy today’s model may fail under its replacement.

The paper proposes RObust Algorithmic Recourse, or ROAR, to account for model shifts when constructing advice. It uses adversarial training to find recourses that are robust to those shifts. This makes the stability of the recommendation part of the optimization problem, addressing the possibility that someone acts on advice whose predictive basis later changes.

The theoretical analysis quantifies the probability that recourse generated without considering model shifts becomes invalid. It also proves a bound on the additional cost of robust recourses produced by the framework. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. Together, the results examine both sides of the problem: the risk of fragile advice and the extra cost associated with making advice more robust.
neurips-2021-towards-robust-and-reliable.tldr: ROAR uses adversarial training to produce recourse that is robust to model shifts and provides a bound on its additional cost.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning becomes expensive when each training run involves a very large neural network. This paper shows that, under Maximal Update Parametrization, or μP, many optimal hyperparameters remain stable as model size changes. That stability creates an opportunity to perform the search on a smaller and cheaper model.

The resulting method, μTransfer, parametrizes the target network in μP, tunes hyperparameters on a smaller network, and transfers them without directly tuning the full-sized model. The authors verify the approach on Transformers and ResNets. The claim concerns many hyperparameters under this parametrization, rather than every hyperparameter under arbitrary model scaling.

One demonstration transfers pretraining hyperparameters from a 13-million-parameter model and exceeds published BERT-large results, with total tuning cost equivalent to one BERT-large pretraining run. Another transfers from 40 million parameters and exceeds published results for the 6.7-billion-parameter GPT-3 model, with tuning costing 7% of total pretraining. These examples show how stable hyperparameters can translate into substantial savings while retaining strong performance.
neurips-2021-tuning-large-neural-network.tldr: μTransfer tunes many hyperparameters on small μP-parametrized networks and transfers them to larger models without directly tuning the larger models.
